data.title: Warts (verruca) — viva
data.summary: Viral infections · 15 viva questions with answers
data.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Warts (verruca)** (Viral infections)_

**Q1. What are warts? Name the virus.**
- Benign epidermal proliferations caused by human papillomavirus (HPV) — non-enveloped double-stranded circular DNA virus, Papillomaviridae; >200 types
- Infects basal keratinocytes through micro-abrasions; replicates as cells differentiate; causes koilocytes

**Q2. Classify cutaneous and mucosal warts with HPV types.**
- Common warts (verruca vulgaris): HPV 2, 4 (27, 57)
- Plantar (myrmecia, deep): HPV 1; mosaic plantar: HPV 2
- Plane (flat) warts: HPV 3, 10
- Butcher's warts: HPV 7
- Anogenital warts (condyloma acuminata): HPV 6, 11 (low risk) — high-risk 16, 18, 31, 33 cause intraepithelial neoplasia
- Epidermodysplasia verruciformis: HPV 5, 8 (beta-HPV)
- Oral: focal epithelial hyperplasia (Heck's disease) HPV 13, 32; recurrent respiratory papillomatosis HPV 6, 11
- Bowenoid papulosis and Buschke–Löwenstein tumour (giant condyloma, HPV 6, 11)

**Q3. Describe the clinical types.**
- Common: rough hyperkeratotic papules, fingers/hands/knees; periungual (nail biters); filiform on face/neck
- Plantar: inward-growing painful papule with surrounding callus; interrupted dermatoglyphics; black dots (thrombosed capillaries) on paring
- Plane: flat-topped smooth skin-coloured or brown papules on face/backs of hands; linear in scratch lines (Koebner/pseudo-Koebner)
- Anogenital: soft papillomatous, sessile or pedunculated papules (cauliflower-like)

**Q4. How do you differentiate a plantar wart from a corn (clavus)?**
- Wart: interrupts skin lines, black dots on paring, pain on lateral squeeze (pinching), multiple, not necessarily on pressure points
- Corn: skin lines pass through, central translucent core, no black dots, pain on direct pressure, at pressure points

**Q5. Histopathology of a wart?**
- Hyperkeratosis with parakeratosis in columns over papillomatous peaks, acanthosis, elongated rete ridges bending inwards ('arborisation')
- Koilocytes (vacuolated keratinocytes with pyknotic nucleus and perinuclear halo) in upper spinous/granular layer, coarse keratohyaline granules, dilated capillaries in dermal papillae
- Myrmecia: large eosinophilic intracytoplasmic inclusions

**Q6. Differential diagnosis.**
- Common: seborrhoeic keratosis, actinic keratosis, SCC/keratoacanthoma, molluscum, TBVC, lichen planus hypertrophic, acrokeratosis verruciformis of Hopf
- Plane: lichen planus, lichen nitidus, syringomas, epidermodysplasia verruciformis, milia
- Genital: pearly penile papules, Fordyce spots, vestibular papillae, condyloma lata (secondary syphilis — moist, flat), molluscum, bowenoid papulosis, seborrhoeic keratosis

**Q7. Treatment options — classify.**
- Destructive: chemical — salicylic acid 12–26%/lactic acid (first line, cheap), trichloroacetic acid, podophyllin 20–25%/podophyllotoxin 0.5% (genital; not in pregnancy), cantharidin, glutaraldehyde, formaldehyde
- Physical — cryotherapy (liquid nitrogen, every 2–3 weeks), electrocautery/radiofrequency ablation, curettage, CO2/Er:YAG laser, pulsed-dye laser
- Antiproliferative: 5-fluorouracil, bleomycin intralesional, cidofovir, retinoids (plane warts)
- Immunotherapy: imiquimod 5% (genital), sinecatechins, contact sensitisers (DPCP, SADBE), intralesional antigens (MMR, Candida, PPD, Mw vaccine, vitamin D3), oral zinc, cimetidine (weak evidence)

**Q8. What is intralesional immunotherapy? Mention the principle.**
- Injecting an antigen (MMR vaccine, Candida antigen, PPD, Mycobacterium w/MIP, vitamin D3) into one or a few warts induces a Th1 cell-mediated response that clears distant untreated warts too
- Useful for multiple, recalcitrant warts; side effects — pain, flu-like illness; avoid in immunosuppressed and pregnancy (live vaccines)

**Q9. Management of anogenital warts.**
- Patient-applied: podophyllotoxin 0.5% solution/0.15% cream (3 days on, 4 off, up to 4 cycles), imiquimod 5% (3 nights/week up to 16 weeks), sinecatechins 15%
- Provider: cryotherapy, TCA 80–90%, podophyllin 25%, electrocautery, excision, laser
- Pregnancy: cryotherapy/TCA/excision — avoid podophyllin, imiquimod relatively avoided
- Screen for other STIs, examine partner, Pap smear in women; condom use
- In children — consider sexual abuse but also non-sexual (vertical, autoinoculation, hetero-inoculation)

**Q10. What is epidermodysplasia verruciformis? (short note)**
- Rare inherited (mostly autosomal recessive — TMC6/EVER1, TMC8/EVER2, CIB1) susceptibility to beta-HPV (5, 8)
- Widespread plane-wart-like papules and pityriasis versicolor-like macules from childhood
- ~30–60% develop SCC on sun-exposed skin in 4th–5th decade — strict photoprotection; acquired form in HIV/transplant

**Q11. Which HPV vaccines are available? Schedule?**
- Bivalent (16, 18), quadrivalent (6, 11, 16, 18), nonavalent (adds 31, 33, 45, 52, 58), Indian quadrivalent Cervavac (Serum Institute, 2022)
- Best before sexual debut — 9–14 years: 2 doses 6 months apart; ≥15 y: 3 doses (0, 1–2, 6 months); WHO now also allows single dose
- India: HPV vaccination for girls 9–14 years announced for national programme

**Q12. Why are warts common and recalcitrant in transplant recipients?**
- Impaired cell-mediated immunity; HPV persists and lesions progress to SCC (beta-HPV with UV as co-factor)

**Q13. What is Buschke–Löwenstein tumour?**
- Giant condyloma acuminatum (HPV 6/11) — locally destructive, verrucous carcinoma-like; treat with wide surgical excision

**Q14. What is bowenoid papulosis?**
- Multiple small reddish-brown flat papules on genitals of young adults (HPV 16) — histology of SCC in situ, behaviour usually benign; partners risk cervical neoplasia

**Q15. Prognosis of untreated common warts?**
- About two-thirds of warts in children resolve spontaneously within 2 years; regression may show blackening

## Quick spotter facts
- Black dots + interrupted dermatoglyphics — plantar wart
- Koilocytes — HPV
- HPV 5, 8 — epidermodysplasia verruciformis with SCC risk

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Viral infections — HPV). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._
